title: Blood Cell Breakdown: Red Cell Removal, Bilirubin, Hemolysis, and Iron
subject: Hematologic System (HEME)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows blood cells from the end of their lives to the recycling of their parts. It explains why red cells survive about 120 days and how macrophages remove them, how heme becomes bilirubin and leaves the body, how laboratory findings reveal whether red cells are destroyed inside vessels or inside macrophages, how iron is absorbed and recycled under the control of hepcidin, and why blood counts fall in a fixed order when the marrow stops. Board questions usually give bilirubin fractions, urine findings, haptoglobin, iron studies, or a post-chemotherapy blood count and ask for the mechanism. Most answers come back to where a cell is destroyed, how water soluble a pigment is, or how long a cell lives.
prerequisites: Red cell structure, hemoglobin, and erythropoiesis (HE-1, HE-2)

connections.how: Hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and autoimmune hemolysis are recognized by the intravascular and extravascular patterns taught here.
Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, and aplastic anemia are explained by iron handling, hepcidin, and circulating life span.
Bilirubin fractions and urine findings locate jaundice before, within, or after the hepatocyte, and chronic hemolysis forms black pigment gallstones.
Whether antibody and complement complete the membrane attack complex decides whether red cells lyse in vessels or are eaten by macrophages.
Interleukin 6 induction of hepcidin links inflammation to low serum iron and iron-restricted red cell production.

sections.title: Red cell life span and removal of senescent cells

blocks.text: Mature red cells have no nucleus, ribosomes, or mitochondria. They make ATP only by glycolysis and NADPH only through the pentose phosphate pathway, and they cannot synthesize new protein. Every enzyme and membrane protein the cell will ever have is present when it leaves the marrow, so function declines steadily as these proteins are oxidized and lost. In healthy adults this gives a fairly uniform life span of about 120 days.

Aging makes the cell both easier to recognize and harder to squeeze through narrow spaces. Enzyme activity, including glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, falls, so oxidant defense weakens. The cell sheds membrane in small vesicles, losing surface area relative to volume, and becomes denser and less deformable. Oxidized band 3 protein clusters and binds naturally occurring IgG and complement C3 fragments, and phosphatidylserine moves from the inner to the outer membrane leaflet. Each of these changes is a signal for phagocytosis.

The spleen is the main quality-control site. In the open circulation of the red pulp, blood percolates through the splenic cords and must re-enter the venous sinuses through narrow slits between endothelial cells, only about 1 to 2 µm wide, while a red cell is about 7 to 8 µm across. A young, deformable cell folds through. A stiff old cell is held in the cords, where slow flow, low glucose, and low pH prolong its contact with cord macrophages, which engulf it (culling). Splenic macrophages can also remove rigid inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies and Heinz bodies and return the cell to the circulation (pitting). Kupffer cells in the liver and marrow macrophages remove the remaining old cells, and the liver becomes the dominant site when cells are heavily coated with complement or the spleen is absent.

steps: No nucleus or ribosomes: damaged proteins are not replaced

Clustered band 3 binds IgG and C3; phosphatidylserine exposed
Stiff cell trapped in splenic cords at the sinus slits
Cord macrophage engulfs the cell
Globin to amino acids, iron to transferrin, heme to bilirubin
blocks.caption: Loss of deformability traps the cell, and surface changes mark it for phagocytosis; liver and marrow macrophages handle the remainder.

blocks.text: Inside the phagolysosome, globin is hydrolyzed to amino acids that return to the plasma pool, iron is released from heme and exported to transferrin, and the porphyrin ring is converted to bilirubin (C02). About 1% of red cells, roughly 200 billion cells carrying about 6 g of hemoglobin, are removed each day and matched by marrow output, reflected in a reticulocyte count of about 0.5% to 2%. This recycling returns about 20 to 25 mg of iron a day, far more than the 1 to 2 mg absorbed from food (C04).

Removing the spleen changes red cell survival little, because the liver takes over culling, but pitting is lost, so Howell-Jolly bodies, Pappenheimer bodies, and target cells appear on the smear. An enlarged, congested spleen does the opposite: it traps and destroys more cells, including normal ones, and pools platelets (hypersplenism).

sections.title: Heme catabolism and the bilirubin pathway

blocks.text: Adults produce about 250 to 350 mg of bilirubin a day, about 80% from hemoglobin of senescent red cells and the rest from ineffective erythropoiesis and other heme proteins such as myoglobin and cytochromes. Each step changes water solubility, which decides where the pigment can travel and which body fluid it can enter.
Formation in macrophages

Microsomal heme oxygenase, using O2 and NADPH, opens the porphyrin ring at the alpha-methene bridge. The products are green biliverdin, ferrous iron, and carbon monoxide; heme breakdown is the main endogenous source of CO, which is why carboxyhemoglobin rises slightly in brisk hemolysis. Cytosolic biliverdin reductase, also using NADPH, then reduces biliverdin to yellow-orange unconjugated bilirubin.
Transport and the danger of free bilirubin

Internal hydrogen bonds fold the bilirubin molecule and hide its polar groups, so unconjugated bilirubin is nearly insoluble in water and soluble in lipid. It travels in plasma tightly bound to albumin, which keeps it out of the glomerular filtrate, so it never appears in urine. The small unbound fraction crosses membranes, including the blood-brain barrier; at high levels in newborns it deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei (kernicterus). Low albumin, or competitors for its binding site such as sulfonamides, salicylates, and free fatty acids, raise the free fraction.
Hepatic uptake, conjugation, and secretion

Hepatocytes take up bilirubin across the sinusoidal membrane by carrier-mediated transport and hold it with cytosolic binding proteins (ligandin, a glutathione S-transferase). In the endoplasmic reticulum, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid, forming mainly bilirubin diglucuronide. The ATP-dependent canalicular pump MRP2 secretes conjugated bilirubin into bile against a steep gradient. This secretion step is rate limiting, so when hepatocytes are injured, conjugated bilirubin refluxes into blood. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and only loosely bound to albumin, so it is filtered and appears in urine whenever its plasma level rises.
Intestinal conversion and excretion

Conjugated bilirubin is not absorbed in the small intestine. In the terminal ileum and colon, bacterial beta-glucuronidases remove the glucuronide and bacteria reduce the pigment to colorless urobilinogen. Most is converted through stercobilinogen to stercobilin, which colors stool brown. About 10% to 20% of urobilinogen is reabsorbed into portal blood; the liver takes up and re-excretes most of it, and a small amount is filtered by the kidney and oxidized to yellow urobilin in urine. The laboratory reports conjugated bilirubin as direct, because it reacts directly with the diazo reagent, and unconjugated as indirect. Total serum bilirubin is normally about 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL (about 5 to 21 µmol/L), and scleral jaundice becomes visible at about 2 to 3 mg/dL.

blocks.predict: A stone completely blocks the common bile duct. Predict urine bilirubin, urine urobilinogen, and stool color.
blocks.explain: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood and, being water soluble, is filtered, so urine bilirubin is positive and urine is dark. No bilirubin reaches the gut, so bacteria form no urobilinogen or stercobilin: urine urobilinogen is absent and stools are pale.

blocks.text: Hemolysis means red cell survival shorter than about 120 days. Whether cells are destroyed inside macrophages (extravascular hemolysis) or burst within the circulation (intravascular hemolysis) decides which laboratory markers change. Most hemolysis is extravascular, and many disorders combine both, so findings identify the dominant site.
Findings shared by both patterns

Any increase in destruction raises the heme load, so unconjugated bilirubin rises, usually modestly (rarely above about 4 to 5 mg/dL without liver disease), because a healthy liver can conjugate several times its usual load. Urine urobilinogen increases while urine bilirubin stays negative, and long-standing hemolysis concentrates bilirubin in bile, where calcium bilirubinate precipitates as black pigment gallstones. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), abundant in red cells as LDH-1 and LDH-2, leaks out with destruction and is generally highest in intravascular hemolysis. A healthy marrow responds with reticulocytosis.
Intravascular hemolysis

When a red cell ruptures in the circulation, hemoglobin tetramers split into alpha-beta dimers, which haptoglobin, a liver-made plasma glycoprotein, binds with very high affinity. Macrophages, mainly in the liver, clear the complex through the CD163 receptor, so haptoglobin is consumed faster than it is made and falls to very low or undetectable levels. Once haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin turns plasma pink to red (hemoglobinemia), and released heme is bound by hemopexin. Free dimers (about 32 kDa) pass the glomerular filter and are reabsorbed by proximal tubule cells, which store the iron as ferritin and hemosiderin. When reabsorption is exceeded, hemoglobinuria appears: red to brown urine that is dipstick positive for blood with few or no red cells on microscopy. Tubule cells loaded with hemosiderin are shed days later, so hemosiderinuria, shown by Prussian blue staining of urine sediment, marks recurrent or chronic intravascular hemolysis even between episodes. Free hemoglobin also scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle spasm, and large loads injure tubules.
Extravascular hemolysis

In extravascular hemolysis, macrophages of the spleen and liver ingest red cells and degrade the hemoglobin inside, so little reaches plasma. Haptoglobin is normal or moderately reduced, and the urine contains no hemoglobin or hemosiderin. Cells coated with warm IgG lose membrane when splenic macrophages remove pieces through Fc receptors, and cells with defective cytoskeletal proteins in hereditary spherocytosis shed membrane vesicles. Either way, surface area falls relative to volume, the cell becomes a spherocyte, and it is trapped in the splenic cords; the extra work enlarges the spleen. Complement adds a distinction: a completed membrane attack complex (ABO antibodies) lyses cells in vessels, whereas cells carrying only C3b (cold agglutinin disease) are cleared mainly by liver macrophages.

blocks.title: Intravascular versus extravascular hemolysis
rows: Schistocytes when mechanical shear is the cause
ABO-incompatible transfusion, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, microangiopathic hemolysis (TTP, HUS, DIC), mechanical heart valve
Hereditary spherocytosis, warm autoimmune hemolysis, thalassemia, sickle cell disease (mostly)
blocks.caption: Shared markers confirm hemolysis; haptoglobin, plasma, and urine locate it.

blocks.title: Locating hemolysis from the laboratory
blocks.text: A 62-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve has hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, reticulocytes 6%, LDH three times the upper limit, indirect bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, and undetectable haptoglobin. Urine is dipstick positive for blood without red cells, and the sediment stains with Prussian blue. Step 1: reticulocytosis with high LDH and indirect bilirubin means hemolysis with a responsive marrow. Step 2: absent haptoglobin with hemoglobinuria means free hemoglobin in plasma, so destruction is intravascular. Step 3: hemosiderinuria means it has continued for days or longer. Step 4: schistocytes on the smear would confirm mechanical shear by the valve. Warm autoimmune hemolysis would instead show spherocytes, a positive direct antiglobulin test, splenomegaly, and urine free of hemoglobin.

sections.title: Iron absorption, transport, storage, and hepcidin

blocks.text: The body contains about 3 to 4 g of iron, roughly two thirds in hemoglobin and most of the rest stored as ferritin and hemosiderin in liver, spleen, and marrow. Free iron catalyzes hydroxyl radical formation (the Fenton reaction), yet there is no regulated way to excrete it; only about 1 to 2 mg a day is lost in shed cells and minor bleeding. Balance is therefore controlled where iron enters plasma.
Absorption

A typical diet supplies about 10 to 20 mg a day; about 10% is absorbed, mainly in the duodenum. Nonheme iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+), poorly soluble above the acidic pH of the stomach. Duodenal cytochrome b on the brush border reduces it to ferrous (Fe2+) iron, aided by acid and ascorbate, and divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) carries Fe2+ into the enterocyte coupled to H+. Heme iron is absorbed more efficiently by a separate, incompletely characterized route and freed inside the cell by heme oxygenase. Inside the enterocyte, iron is either stored in ferritin, and lost when the cell is shed a few days later, or exported across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin. The copper-containing ferroxidase hephaestin oxidizes it back to Fe3+ for binding to transferrin; plasma ceruloplasmin does the same for iron leaving macrophages and hepatocytes.
Transport and storage

Transferrin carries two Fe3+ ions per molecule. Erythroid precursors take up iron-loaded transferrin through transferrin receptor 1 by endocytosis, release the iron in the acidified endosome, and send it to mitochondria, where ferrochelatase inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX. Ferritin, a hollow 24-subunit shell, stores Fe3+ in soluble, nontoxic form; hemosiderin is aggregated, partly degraded ferritin.
Hepcidin

Hepcidin, a 25-amino-acid hepatocyte peptide, binds ferroportin and causes its internalization and degradation, trapping iron in enterocytes, macrophages, and hepatocytes. Hepatocytes raise hepcidin when transferrin saturation and liver iron rise (sensed through HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and BMP6 signaling) and when interleukin 6 activates JAK-STAT3 in inflammation. Hepcidin falls with iron deficiency, hypoxia, and active erythropoiesis, when erythropoietin-stimulated erythroblasts secrete erythroferrone.

blocks.caption: Negative feedback on iron entry into plasma.

blocks.text: Inflammation raises hepcidin regardless of stores, locking iron in macrophages, so serum iron falls while ferritin is normal or high (anemia of chronic disease). In hereditary hemochromatosis, HFE mutations (most often homozygous C282Y) blunt hepcidin, so absorption continues despite overload and iron deposits in liver, pancreas, heart, and joints. In ineffective erythropoiesis, as in beta-thalassemia, erythroferrone suppresses hepcidin and iron overload develops even without transfusion.

blocks.title: Iron studies and what they reflect
blocks.caption: Hepatocytes make more transferrin when iron is scarce, so TIBC rises in deficiency and falls in inflammation.

blocks.title: Is iron absent or locked away?
blocks.text: In active rheumatoid arthritis: hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, serum iron 35 µg/dL, TIBC 220 µg/dL, saturation 16%, ferritin 180 ng/mL. Low serum iron does not separate the causes; TIBC does. Deficiency would raise TIBC, but here it is low, and ferritin shows stores are present, so IL-6-driven hepcidin is trapping iron in macrophages. Because ferritin rises with inflammation, a value below about 100 ng/mL here would suggest coexisting deficiency.

sections.title: Circulating life span and the order of cytopenias after marrow suppression

blocks.text: Each blood count is a steady state: the number of cells in the blood equals the rate of production multiplied by the time each cell spends there. When production stops abruptly, as after cytotoxic chemotherapy, high-dose radiation, or drug-induced marrow aplasia, cells already in the blood keep aging out at their normal rate with no replacements. Each count then falls on a timescale set by the cell's circulating life span and by the marrow's reserve of finished cells.

Neutrophils circulate with a half-life of only about 6 to 8 hours before migrating into tissues, where they survive a day or two more. The marrow holds a storage pool of mature and band neutrophils many times larger than the circulating pool, which buffers the count for several days and is released quickly by stress, glucocorticoids, or granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Once that pool is spent, the absolute neutrophil count (normally about 1,500 to 7,000 per µL) falls steeply, reaching its lowest point about 7 to 14 days after typical cytotoxic regimens. Below about 500 per µL the risk of bacterial and fungal infection rises sharply, and signs of inflammation may be muted because few cells are present to form pus.

Platelets survive about 7 to 10 days, and about one third are held in the spleen at any time. Thrombocytopenia therefore follows the neutropenia over about 1 to 2 weeks. Thrombopoietin is made by the liver at a fairly constant rate and is removed by binding to platelets and megakaryocytes, so its plasma level rises as the platelet mass falls. Low platelets cause petechiae and mucosal bleeding, with spontaneous bleeding more likely below about 10,000 to 20,000 per µL (normal about 150,000 to 400,000 per µL).

Red cells last about 120 days, so with production halted the red cell mass falls by only about 1% a day and hemoglobin drifts down over weeks. The earliest red cell sign is a fall in the reticulocyte count, because reticulocytes mature within about a day in the blood. A patient after chemotherapy therefore presents with fever from neutropenia, or with bleeding, well before significant anemia. Anemia appears early only when blood is also lost or destroyed.

Falls second, over about 1 to 2 weeks

blocks.caption: The shorter the circulating life, the sooner the count falls once production stops.

blocks.text: Lymphocytes are the exception: although long lived, they fall within about 24 to 48 hours of significant radiation because radiation kills them directly by apoptosis, not because production stops. The same life span logic also explains why a short pause in red cell production is dangerous only when red cell survival is already short.

blocks.predict: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors and halts red cell production for about a week. Predict the hemoglobin change in a healthy adult and in a patient with sickle cell disease, whose red cells survive about 10 to 20 days.
blocks.explain: The healthy adult loses about 1% of red cell mass a day, roughly 7% over the week, which goes unnoticed. The sickle cell patient loses about 5% to 10% a day with no replacement, so hemoglobin falls steeply within days (transient aplastic crisis), with a reticulocyte count near zero.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology set the stage: the open circulation of the splenic red pulp tests red cell deformability, Kupffer cells line the hepatic sinusoids, the polarized hepatocyte takes up bilirubin at one face and secretes it at the canaliculus, and the proximal tubule reabsorbs filtered hemoglobin. Biochemistry supplies the chemistry of heme oxygenase, UGT1A1, and MRP2, whose inherited defects (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar, and Dubin-Johnson syndromes) are distinguished by which bilirubin fraction rises. Immunology decides where antibody-coated cells die, depending on whether IgG engages splenic Fc receptors or complement completes the membrane attack complex, and IL-6 connects inflammation to hepcidin and iron sequestration.

Pathology applies these mechanisms but rarely in pure form. Sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency, and malaria mix intravascular and extravascular destruction; haptoglobin is also an acute phase reactant and falls in liver disease; and ferritin rises with inflammation, liver injury, and malignancy. Laboratory patterns are therefore read together with the smear rather than from a single value. Life span reasoning carries into microbiology and oncology, explaining why parvovirus B19 is dangerous in hemolytic disease and why infection risk after chemotherapy peaks before anemia appears.

summary: Red cells lack a nucleus and ribosomes, so they cannot replace damaged proteins; they stiffen and are culled by splenic macrophages after about 120 days.
Heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin, Fe2+, and CO; biliverdin reductase forms water-insoluble unconjugated bilirubin carried on albumin.
UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid; MRP2 secretion into bile is the rate-limiting step, and only conjugated bilirubin can enter urine.
Gut bacteria form urobilinogen, which becomes stercobilin in stool and urobilin in urine; complete biliary obstruction removes both.
LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, urine urobilinogen, and reticulocytes rise in all hemolysis; very low haptoglobin, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and hemosiderinuria mark intravascular destruction.
Schistocytes point to mechanical intravascular hemolysis; spherocytes and splenomegaly point to extravascular hemolysis.
Duodenal cytochrome b reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ for DMT1 uptake; ferroportin exports iron, hephaestin and ceruloplasmin reoxidize it, and transferrin carries it.
Hepcidin degrades ferroportin; inflammation raises it (anemia of chronic disease), while iron deficiency, hypoxia, and erythropoiesis lower it, and HFE mutations keep it inappropriately low.
Iron deficiency raises TIBC and lowers ferritin; anemia of chronic disease lowers TIBC with normal or high ferritin.
After abrupt marrow failure, neutrophils (hours) fall first, platelets (7 to 10 days) next, and hemoglobin (120 days) last.

verify: The width of the interendothelial slits of splenic sinuses is quoted from about 0.5 to 3 µm in different sources; this chapter uses about 1 to 2 µm.
Reference ranges for total bilirubin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, ferritin, ANC, and platelets vary between laboratories and texts; confirm the values NABNE uses.
The statement that hemolysis alone rarely raises bilirubin above about 4 to 5 mg/dL follows common clinical teaching; confirm the threshold NABNE expects.
Neutrophil circulating half-life is usually taught as about 6 to 8 hours, but some isotope labeling studies suggest longer survival; this chapter uses the classic value.
The intestinal transporter for heme iron is not established; confirm whether NABNE expects a named transporter.
Some texts describe the iron released by heme oxygenase as ferric rather than ferrous (used here); confirm.
The ferritin level that suggests coexisting iron deficiency during inflammation (about 100 ng/mL here) differs among guidelines.
Timing of neutrophil and platelet nadirs after chemotherapy depends on the agent; the ranges given are typical, not fixed.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the terms culling and pitting, the eponyms cords of Billroth, and the names erythroferrone and hephaestin.
